title: A stack in a fixed array

prereqs.why: You are building the structure, so what it does and does not allow is the specification.
The storage is a fixed-size vector used as a raw array - no push_back, because the growing is the part you are doing by hand.
Every operation has to refuse to run off either end, and the index of the top is one off from the count.

statement:
Implement a **fixed-capacity** stack of integers backed by an array. Do not use
`std::stack`, `push_back`, `list.append` or anything that grows for you -
allocate `cap` slots once and manage a count yourself.

First line: `cap m` - the capacity and the number of commands. Then `m`
commands, one of:

| Command | Print | When it cannot |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `push <x>` | `push ok` | `push full` if already at capacity |
| `pop` | `pop <value>` | `pop empty` |
| `top` | `top <value>` | `top empty` |
| `size` | `size <n>` | - |

```
input:   2 7              output:  push ok
         push 10                   push ok
         push 20                   push full
         push 30                   top 20
         top                       pop 20
         pop                       top 10
         top                       size 1
         size
```

A full stack **rejects** the push and keeps its contents; it does not overwrite
anything. A pop removes the value it reports.

### The point of the problem

Three lines of state - the buffer, the capacity, and how many slots are in use -
and the only thing that makes it correct is being consistent about what the
count means.

Keep `count` as **the number of elements**, which makes `buf[count]` the next
free slot and `buf[count - 1]` the top. That is the half-open convention again:
the push site is `count`, the top is one below it, and `count == 0` is empty with
no subtraction anywhere near it.

The other common choice is a `top` index that points *at* the top element and
sits at `-1` when empty. It works, and it needs a signed type, and every
expression that uses it is one off from the version above. Pick one and be
consistent - the bugs come from a function written in one convention sitting
next to a function written in the other.

### Boundary cases

Every operation on an empty stack. Pushing exactly to capacity, then one more.
Filling, emptying completely, and filling again - which catches an
implementation that leaves stale state behind. A capacity of 0, where every push
is immediately `full`. A capacity of 1. Popping below empty repeatedly.

### Platform assumptions

`cap` is between 0 and 1000, `m` is at most 5000, and values fit in a 32-bit
`int`. `count` is a `std::size_t`, so the comparison against `buf.size()` needs
no cast. Commands are always well formed, so you do not have to handle an
unknown command word.
hints: Allocate once: `std::vector<int> buf(cap, 0);` gives exactly `cap` slots that already exist. From then on you only ever assign to `buf[i]` - never `push_back`, which would grow past the capacity you are supposed to be enforcing.
Push is `if (count == buf.size()) full; else { buf[count] = x; ++count; }`. Pop is the mirror image: `--count;` first, then read `buf[count]` - which is the element that was on top.
`top` is `buf[count - 1]`, and that subtraction is only safe because you checked `count == 0` first. Check emptiness before computing any index, not after.

cases.stdin:
2 7
push 10
push 20
push 30
top
pop
top
size
cases.expect:
push ok
push ok
push full
top 20
pop 20
top 10
